items.title: Central-force trajectories: the central-force equation, angular momentum, energy and the effective potential
items.design_state: completed-local-argument (M9 split into items; new local prerequisites recorded in the batch notes)
items.statement:
Let $\mu>0$ be a real number, let $J_0\subseteq(0,\infty)$ be an open interval,
let $U:J_0\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be
an interval with at least two points ([[def-interval]]), and let
$r:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be twice differentiable with $|r(t)|\in J_0$ for every
$t\in I$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). The curve $r$ is a
**central-force trajectory for** $(\mu,U)$ when

$$\mu\,r''(t)=-\frac{U'(|r(t)|)}{|r(t)|}\,r(t)\qquad(t\in I),$$

where $|x|:=\lVert x\rVert_2$ is the Euclidean norm
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) and $U'$ is the derivative of $U$ on the
open interval $J_0$.

**Attached objects.** The **angular momentum vector** of such a trajectory is
the curve $j:I\to\mathbb R^3$,

$$j(t):=\mu\,r(t)\times r'(t),$$

with $\times$ the cross product of $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]);
its **energy** is the function $E:I\to\mathbb R$,

$$E(t):=\tfrac12\mu\,\lVert r'(t)\rVert_2^2+U(|r(t)|);$$

and for every $J\ge0$ the **effective potential of momentum magnitude** $J$ is
the function $U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J:J_0\to\mathbb R$,

$$U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J(\rho):=U(\rho)+\frac{J^2}{2\mu\,\rho^2}.$$

**Why the objects are defined.** Since $\rho>0$ throughout $J_0$, the right-hand
side of the central-force equation is defined, the map
$\rho\mapsto J^2/(2\mu\rho^2)$ is $C^2$ on $(0,\infty)$ (a quotient of $C^2$
functions with nowhere vanishing denominator), and $U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J$ is
again $C^2$; in particular second derivatives of $U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J$ are
available. The vector $j(t)$ is defined for every $t\in I$ because $r$ is
differentiable there.

**Mathematical status.** The data $\mu$, $U$ and $J$ are real numbers and
functions; the equation and the attached objects are mathematical statements
about curves. Nothing here asserts that the equation describes a physical
interaction, and the names are conventional labels for the mathematical
objects only.

references.title: David Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge), §2.5.4, printed pp. 31-33, Eqs. (2.82)-(2.89): two-body reduction, the conserved $J=\mu r^2\dot\phi$, the radial equation and the effective potential $V_{\rm eff}(r)=V(r)+J^2/(2\mu r^2)$
Konstantin Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Classical Mechanics, §3.4, Eqs. (3.44)-(3.65): motion in a central field, the first integral and the effective potential

items.title: Local polar coordinates for a curve with nonvanishing position in the plane: a differentiable angle function with prescribed derivative
items.design_state: completed-local-argument (M9 split into items; new local prerequisites recorded in the batch notes)
items.statement:
Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two points
([[def-interval]]), let $t_0\in I$, and let $\rho,\sigma:I\to\mathbb R$ be twice
differentiable ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) with
$(\rho(t),\sigma(t))\ne(0,0)$ for every $t\in I$. Put

$$r(t):=\sqrt{\rho(t)^2+\sigma(t)^2}>0\qquad(t\in I).$$

Then there is a twice differentiable $\theta:I\to\mathbb R$ with

$$\rho=r\cos\theta,\qquad\sigma=r\sin\theta\qquad\text{on }I,$$

and every twice differentiable $\vartheta:I\to\mathbb R$ with
$\rho=r\cos\vartheta$ and $\sigma=r\sin\vartheta$ on $I$ satisfies

$$\vartheta'(t)=\frac{\rho(t)\sigma'(t)-\sigma(t)\rho'(t)}{r(t)^2}\qquad(t\in I).$$

references.title: David Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge), §2.5.4, printed p. 31, Eqs. (2.83)-(2.84): polar coordinates in the orbital plane and the conserved $J=\mu r^2\dot\phi$

Richard Fitzpatrick, Newtonian Dynamics (University of Texas at Austin), §6.3 Motion in a General Central Force-Field: use of polar coordinates $(r,\theta)$ in the orbital plane with the angular first integral

items.title: Solutions of $v''+\omega^2v=0$ are exactly the functions $A\cos(\omega(t-t_0))+B\sin(\omega(t-t_0))$
items.design_state: completed-local-argument (M9 split into items; new local prerequisites recorded in the batch notes)
items.statement:
Let $\omega>0$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two points
([[def-interval]]), let $t_0\in I$, and let $v:I\to\mathbb R$ be twice
differentiable ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) with

$$v''(t)+\omega^2v(t)=0\qquad(t\in I).$$

Then there are reals $A,B$ with

$$v(t)=A\cos\bigl(\omega(t-t_0)\bigr)+B\sin\bigl(\omega(t-t_0)\bigr)\qquad(t\in I).$$

Conversely, for all reals $A,B$ the function
$t\mapsto A\cos(\omega(t-t_0))+B\sin(\omega(t-t_0))$ is twice differentiable on
$\mathbb R$ and satisfies $v''+\omega^2v=0$ there.

references.title: David Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge), §2.6, printed pp. 38-44: small oscillations and the oscillatory solution with frequency squared $\omega^2$
Konstantin Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Classical Mechanics, Ch. 2 small oscillations: the second-order linear oscillator and its general sinusoidal solution

items.title: The vector triple product identity $u\times(v\times w)=\langle u,w\rangle v-\langle u,v\rangle w$
items.design_state: completed-local-argument (M9 split into items; new local prerequisites recorded in the batch notes)
items.statement:
For all $u,v,w\in\mathbb R^3$,
$$u\times(v\times w)=\langle u,w\rangle\,v-\langle u,v\rangle\,w .$$

references.title: David Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge), §1.1, printed pp. 1-2: the vector triple product and the orthonormality identities for the cross product
Richard Fitzpatrick, Newtonian Dynamics (University of Texas at Austin), §2.5 and Appendix A: vector identities for the cross product, including the triple product rule

items.title: Oriented orthonormal triads in $\mathbb R^3$: existence over any unit vector, and the orthonormal expansion with no fourth orthogonal direction
items.design_state: completed-local-argument (M9 split into items; new local prerequisites recorded in the batch notes)
items.statement:
Call a triple $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of vectors of $\mathbb R^3$ an **oriented
orthonormal triad** when $\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}$ for all
$i,j\in\{1,2,3\}$ and $e_1\times e_2=e_3$. Then:

1. **Existence.** For every $e_3\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|e_3|=1$ there are
   $e_1,e_2\in\mathbb R^3$ such that $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an oriented orthonormal
   triad.
2. **Dimension bound.** Every orthonormal list
   $f_1,\dots,f_m\in\mathbb R^3$ (pairwise orthogonal unit vectors) has
   $m\le3$; consequently, for every oriented orthonormal triad $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$
   and every $x\in\mathbb R^3$,
   $$x=\langle x,e_1\rangle e_1+\langle x,e_2\rangle e_2+\langle x,e_3\rangle e_3, \qquad |x|^2=\langle x,e_1\rangle^2+\langle x,e_2\rangle^2+\langle x,e_3\rangle^2 .$$

Throughout, $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ and $|\cdot|$ are the Euclidean inner
product and norm ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), $\times$ is the cross
product ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]), and $s_1,s_2,s_3$ is the standard basis
of $\mathbb R^3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]).

references.title: David Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge), §1.1 and §2.5.4: orthonormal vector triads, the right-handed relation $\mathbf e_1\times\mathbf e_2=\mathbf e_3$ and planar coordinates in the orbital plane

Richard Fitzpatrick, Newtonian Dynamics (University of Texas at Austin), §2.4: Cartesian components, orthonormal bases and the scalar-product expansion $\mathbf a=(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf e_1)\mathbf e_1+(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf e_2)\mathbf e_2$

items.title: Conservation of the angular momentum vector along a central-force trajectory and its orthogonality to position and velocity
items.design_state: completed-local-argument (M9 split into items; new local prerequisites recorded in the batch notes)
items.statement:
Let $\mu>0$, let $J_0\subseteq(0,\infty)$ be an open interval, let
$U:J_0\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval
with at least two points, and let $r:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a central-force
trajectory for $(\mu,U)$ with angular momentum vector
$j=\mu\,r\times r'$ ([[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]]). Then:

1. $j$ is differentiable on $I$ with $j'(t)=0$ for every $t\in I$; hence $j$ is
   constant on $I$;
2. for every $t\in I$, $\langle r(t),j(t)\rangle=0$ and
   $\langle r'(t),j(t)\rangle=0$.

references.title: David Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge), §2.5.4, printed p. 31, Eqs. (2.83)-(2.84): the orbit lies in a plane perpendicular to the conserved angular momentum

Richard Fitzpatrick, Newtonian Dynamics (University of Texas at Austin), §6.3 Motion in a General Central Force-Field, Eqs. (299)-(304): the angular first integral $r^2\dot\theta=h$ in polar coordinates

items.title: Polar reduction of a non-radial central-force trajectory: $\rho^2\theta'=J/\mu$, the effective-potential equation and energy conservation
items.design_state: completed-local-argument (M9 split into items; new local prerequisites recorded in the batch notes)
items.statement:
Let $\mu>0$, let $J_0\subseteq(0,\infty)$ be an open interval, let
$U:J_0\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval
with at least two points, and let $r:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a central-force
trajectory for $(\mu,U)$ whose angular momentum $j=\mu\,r\times r'$ is a nonzero
constant vector ([[thm-cm-central-force-angular-momentum-conservation]]); write
$J:=|j|>0$. Let $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an oriented orthonormal triad with
$e_3=j/J$ ([[lem-cm-oriented-orthonormal-triads]]).

Then there are twice differentiable $\rho:I\to(0,\infty)$ and
$\theta:I\to\mathbb R$ with

$$r(t)=\rho(t)\bigl(\cos\theta(t)\,e_1+\sin\theta(t)\,e_2\bigr)\qquad(t\in I),$$

and for **every** such pair $(\rho,\theta)$:

1. $\rho(t)=|r(t)|$ for all $t$;
2. $\rho^2\theta'=J/\mu$ on $I$, so $\theta'>0$;
3. the effective-potential equation $\mu\rho''=-\bigl(U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J\bigr)'(\rho)$
   holds on $I$, with $U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J=U+J^2/(2\mu\rho^2)$
   ([[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]]);
4. $E:=\frac12\mu\lVert r'\rVert_2^2+U(|r|)$ equals
   $\frac12\mu\rho'^2+U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J(\rho)$ and is constant on $I$.

references.title: David Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge), §2.5.4, printed pp. 31-33, Eqs. (2.83)-(2.88): the planar polar Lagrangian, the conserved $J=\mu r^2\dot\phi$, the radial equation $\mu\ddot r=-\partial_rV_{\rm eff}$ and the energy $E=\frac12\mu\dot r^2+V_{\rm eff}(r)$
Konstantin Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Classical Mechanics, §3.4, Eqs. (3.44)-(3.57): polar coordinates in a central field, the first integral and the effective radial equation

items.title: Circular orbits of a non-radial central-force trajectory: the critical-point condition and the squared frequency of the linearised radial equation
items.design_state: completed-local-argument (M9 split into items; new local prerequisites recorded in the batch notes)
items.statement:
Let $\mu>0$, let $J_0\subseteq(0,\infty)$ be an open interval, let
$U:J_0\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$, let $I$ be an interval with at least two
points, and let $r:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a central-force trajectory for $(\mu,U)$
with constant nonzero angular momentum $j=Je_3$, $J>0$, and polar data
$(\rho,\theta)$ as in [[thm-cm-central-force-polar-reduction]], so that
$\rho^2\theta'=J/\mu$ and $\mu\rho''=-\bigl(U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J\bigr)'(\rho)$ on
$I$. Fix $r_0\in J_0$. Then:

1. **(Necessity.)** If $\rho\equiv r_0$ is constant on $I$, then
   $\bigl(U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J\bigr)'(r_0)=0$ and $\theta'\equiv J/(\mu r_0^2)$
   is constant; the trajectory is the uniform rotation
   $r(t)=r_0(\cos\theta(t)\,e_1+\sin\theta(t)\,e_2)$.
2. **(Existence.)** Conversely, if $\bigl(U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J\bigr)'(r_0)=0$,
   then for every $\theta_0\in\mathbb R$ the curve
   $$r^\circ(t):=r_0\bigl(\cos(\theta_0+\omega t)\,e_1+\sin(\theta_0+\omega t)\,e_2\bigr), \qquad \omega:=\frac{J}{\mu r_0^2},$$
   is a central-force trajectory for $(\mu,U)$ defined on $\mathbb R$, with
   angular momentum $j=Je_3$ and constant energy
   $E=\frac12\mu r_0^2\omega^2+U(r_0)=U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J(r_0)$.
3. **(Linearised radial equation.)** Let $\rho$ be a solution of the reduced
   equation $\mu\rho''=-\bigl(U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J\bigr)'(\rho)$ on $I$ with
   $\bigl(U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J\bigr)'(r_0)=0$, and put
   $\delta:=\rho-r_0$. Then
   $$\mu\delta''=-\bigl(U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J\bigr)''(r_0)\,\delta +g(\delta),\qquad g(x):=\bigl(U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J\bigr)''(r_0)x-\bigl(U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J\bigr)'(r_0+x),$$
   where $g(x)/x\to0$ as $x\to0$; if moreover
   $\bigl(U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J\bigr)''(r_0)>0$, then the associated linearised
   equation $\mu\delta''=-\bigl(U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J\bigr)''(r_0)\delta$ has
   exactly the solutions
   $\delta(t)=A\cos(\omega_{\rm lin}(t-t_0))+B\sin(\omega_{\rm lin}(t-t_0))$
   with $A,B\in\mathbb R$ and $\omega_{\rm lin}:=\sqrt{\bigl(U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J\bigr)''(r_0)/\mu}>0$,
   for any $t_0\in I$. This is a statement about the quadratic radial
   approximation; no nonlinear stability of the circular orbit is asserted.

references.title: David Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge), §2.5.4 and Figure 15, printed pp. 31-33: circular, elliptic and hyperbolic orbits as features of the effective potential $V_{\rm eff}$
Konstantin Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Classical Mechanics, §3.4, Eqs. (3.52)-(3.58): the circular-orbit condition $\mathrm dU_{\rm eff}/\mathrm dr=0$ and small radial oscillations about it

items.title: Binet's equation for the attractive inverse-square field: $\mathrm d^2u/\mathrm d\varphi^2+u=\mu\kappa/J^2$ for $u=1/\rho$
items.design_state: completed-local-argument (M9 split into items; new local prerequisites recorded in the batch notes)
items.statement:
Let $\mu>0$, $\kappa>0$, let $U:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ be $U(\rho):=-\kappa/\rho$
(of class $C^2$), let $I$ be an interval with at least two points, and let
$r:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a central-force trajectory for $(\mu,U)$ with constant
angular momentum $j=Je_3$, $J>0$. Let $(\rho,\theta)$ be polar data as in
[[thm-cm-central-force-polar-reduction]], let $I^\circ$ be the interior of $I$
(a nonempty interval with at least two points, or empty if $I$ is a singleton,
which is excluded), and put $W:=\theta(I^\circ)$, an interval. Then:

1. $\theta:I^\circ\to W$ is a $C^1$ bijection with inverse
   $\sigma:W\to I^\circ$ of class $C^1$, and the function
   $u:=1/(\rho\circ\sigma):W\to(0,\infty)$ is of class $C^2$;
2. on $W$, $u''+u=\mu\kappa/J^2$ (derivatives with respect to the variable of
   $W$);
3. the auxiliary identity $\rho'=-\dfrac{J}{\mu}\,u'\circ\theta$ holds on
   $I^\circ$;
4. the energy satisfies $E=\dfrac{J^2}{2\mu}\bigl((u')^2+u^2\bigr)-\kappa u$ on
   $W$, where $E$ is the constant energy of the trajectory.

references.title: David Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge), §2.5.4, printed pp. 32-33: the inverse-square radial equation and the orbit equation for $r(\phi)$
Konstantin Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Classical Mechanics, §3.4, Eqs. (3.59)-(3.65): the Binet-type equation and the conic solution with eccentricity $e$ for the Coulomb/Kepler potential

items.title: The Kepler orbit equation is a conic: $u=c(1+e\cos(\varphi-\theta_0))$ with $E=(\mu\kappa^2/2J^2)(e^2-1)$
items.design_state: completed-local-argument (M9 split into items; new local prerequisites recorded in the batch notes)
items.statement:
Let $\mu>0$, $\kappa>0$, $U(\rho)=-\kappa/\rho$ on $(0,\infty)$, let
$r:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a central-force trajectory for $(\mu,U)$ with constant
angular momentum $j=Je_3$, $J>0$ and constant energy $E$
([[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]]), and let
$u:W\to(0,\infty)$, $\theta$ and $\sigma$ be as in
[[thm-cm-kepler-binet-equation]], with $W=\theta(I^\circ)$. Write
$c:=\mu\kappa/J^2>0$ and $p:=1/c=J^2/(\mu\kappa)$. Then:

1. there are $e\ge0$ and $\theta_0\in\mathbb R$ with
   $$u(\varphi)=c\bigl(1+e\cos(\varphi-\theta_0)\bigr)\qquad(\varphi\in W),$$
   and for $t\in I^\circ$ accordingly
   $\rho(t)=p/\bigl(1+e\cos(\theta(t)-\theta_0)\bigr)$;
2. the energy and the eccentricity are related by
   $$E=\frac{\mu\kappa^2}{2J^2}\bigl(e^2-1\bigr);$$ consequently
   $E<0\iff e<1$, $E=0\iff e=1$ and $E>0\iff e>1$.

references.title: Konstantin Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Classical Mechanics, §3.4, Eqs. (3.59)-(3.65): the conic $r=p/(1+e\cos\varphi)$ and the eccentricity-energy relation
David Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge), §2.5.4, printed pp. 32-33: elliptic and hyperbolic orbit classes in terms of the sign of the energy for the inverse-square potential

items.title: The one-dimensional action variable of a family of two-simple-turning-point energy levels
items.design_state: completed-local-argument (E6 split into items; recorded in the batch notes)
items.statement:
Let $J_0\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, let $U:J_0\to\mathbb R$ be
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]), let $m>0$, let $E_0<E_1$ be reals, and
let $a,b:(E_0,E_1)\to J_0$ be functions with

$$a(E)<b(E),\qquad U(a(E))=U(b(E))=E,\qquad U(q)<E\ (a(E)<q<b(E)) \qquad(E_0<E<E_1).$$

The **action variable** of this datum is the function
$J_{\mathrm{a}}:(E_0,E_1)\to\mathbb R$,

$$J_{\mathrm{a}}(E):=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{a(E)}^{b(E)}\sqrt{2m\bigl(E-U(q)\bigr)}\;dq,$$

the integral being the Riemann integral on the compact interval
$[a(E),b(E)]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). It is defined because
$q\mapsto\sqrt{2m(E-U(q))}$ is continuous on $[a(E),b(E)]$: the radicand is a
continuous nonnegative function there (it vanishes exactly at the two
endpoints), and the nonnegative square root is continuous
([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

**Reading of the notation.** The interval $[a(E),b(E)]$ is the classically
allowed segment between the two turning points of the energy $E$, and the
integral is twice the momentum phase-space area (Tong, Eq. (4.136) with
$I=J_{\mathrm{a}}$); no physical interpretation of $m$, $U$ or $E$ is a
mathematical premise here, and no period is claimed by this definition.

references.title: David Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge), §4.5.3, printed pp. 108-111, Eqs. (4.133)-(4.142): the action variable $I=\frac{1}{2\pi}\oint p\,dq$ of a one-dimensional system and the identity $\omega=dE/dI$
Konstantin Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Classical Mechanics, §10.4: adiabatic invariants and the action variable of a periodic one-dimensional motion

items.title: The subcritical Kepler conic is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=p/(1-e^2)$, $b=a\sqrt{1-e^2}$, focus at the origin and area $\pi ab$; its area is also $\tfrac12\int_0^{2\pi}\varrho^2$
items.design_state: completed-local-argument (E6 split into items; recorded in the batch notes)
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $p>0$ and
$0\le e<1$, and put
$$a:=\frac{p}{1-e^2}>0,\qquad b:=a\sqrt{1-e^2},\qquad \varrho(\varphi):=\frac{p}{1+e\cos\varphi}\quad(\varphi\in\mathbb R).$$

1. $\varrho$ is $C^1$, $2\pi$-periodic, and
   $\dfrac{p}{1+e}\le\varrho\le\dfrac{p}{1-e}$.
2. Let $Q(x,y):=(1-e^2)x^2+y^2+2pex-p^2$ and
   $E_{\rm ell}:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:Q(x,y)\le0\}$. Then
   $E_{\rm ell}$ is Lebesgue measurable, and for the closed unit disc
   $\overline B\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ and $T(u,v):=(au-ae,bv)$ one has
   $E_{\rm ell}=T[\overline B]$; consequently
   $\lambda_2(E_{\rm ell})=\pi ab=\pi a^2\sqrt{1-e^2}$.
3. For every $\varphi$, the ray $\{s(\cos\varphi,\sin\varphi):s>0\}$ meets
   $\partial E_{\rm ell}$ in the unique point
   $\varrho(\varphi)(\cos\varphi,\sin\varphi)$; that point satisfies
   $Q=0$, and $\lambda_2(E_{\rm ell})=\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}\varrho(\varphi)^2\,
   \mathrm d\varphi$.

Thus the conic $Q=0$ is the ellipse with centre $(-ae,0)$, semiaxes $a,b$,
its right focus at the origin, and enclosed area $\pi ab$.

references.title: Konstantin Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Classical Mechanics, §3.4, Eqs. (3.59)-(3.65) and Fig. 8: the elliptic branch $E<0$, $e<1$, with the turning radii and the ellipse geometry
Richard Fitzpatrick, Newtonian Dynamics (University of Texas at Austin), §5.5 and §5.6: the elliptic orbit of the Kepler problem, its semiaxes and the focus at the force centre

items.title: Completeness and periodicity of the negative-energy Kepler orbit, with $T=2\pi\mu ab/J$ and $T^2=4\pi^2\mu a^3/\kappa$
items.design_state: completed-local-argument (E6 split into items; recorded in the batch notes)
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mu>0$,
$\kappa>0$, $U(\rho)=-\kappa/\rho$ on $(0,\infty)$, and let $r:I\to\mathbb R^3$
be a central-force trajectory for $(\mu,U)$ with constant angular momentum
$j=Je_3$, $J>0$, and constant energy $E<0$. Let $e\in[0,1)$,
$\theta_0\in\mathbb R$, $p=J^2/(\mu\kappa)$, $a=p/(1-e^2)$,
$b=a\sqrt{1-e^2}$, and $\varrho(\varphi):=p/(1+e\cos(\varphi-\theta_0))$
be the conic data of [[thm-cm-kepler-conic-and-eccentricity]], and let
$(\rho,\theta)$ be polar data as in
[[thm-cm-central-force-polar-reduction]]. Then:

1. **(Completeness.)** $r$ extends uniquely to a central-force trajectory for
   $(\mu,U)$ defined on all of $\mathbb R$; along it
   $\rho(t)\in[p/(1+e),\,p/(1-e)]$ for every $t$, and $\rho$ and $\rho'$ are
   bounded. Consequently every maximal central-force trajectory with these
   data has domain $\mathbb R$.
2. **(Periodicity.)** $\theta:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is a strictly increasing
   $C^1$ bijection with
   $\dfrac{J}{\mu}\Bigl(\dfrac{1-e}{p}\Bigr)^2\le\theta'\le\dfrac{J}{\mu}\Bigl(\dfrac{1+e}{p}\Bigr)^2$;
   if $t_0\in\mathbb R$ and $T>0$ is determined by
   $\theta(t_0+T)=\theta(t_0)+2\pi$, then $r(t+T)=r(t)$ and
   $r'(t+T)=r'(t)$ for all $t\in\mathbb R$.
3. **(Period value.)** With $r_{\max}:=p/(1-e)$ and $r_{\min}:=p/(1+e)$,
   $$T=\frac{2\pi\mu ab}{J}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{\kappa}}\,a^{3/2}, \qquad T^2=\frac{4\pi^2\mu a^3}{\kappa}.$$

references.title: David Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge), §2.5.4, printed pp. 32-33, Eqs. (2.86)-(2.90): the $E<0$ elliptic branch of the inverse-square problem
Konstantin Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Classical Mechanics, §3.4, Eqs. (3.59)-(3.65): the elliptic branch and the relation between period, semimajor axis and potential strength

items.title: The action variable of a two-simple-turning-point family is $C^1$ with derivative $T(E)/(2\pi)$, the period quadrature over $2\pi$
items.design_state: completed-local-argument (E6 split into items; recorded in the batch notes)
items.statement:
Let $J_0\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, let $U:J_0\to\mathbb R$ be of
class $C^3$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), let $m>0$, let
$E_0<E_1$, and let $a,b:(E_0,E_1)\to J_0$ be functions with
$a(E)<b(E)$, $U(a(E))=U(b(E))=E$, $U(q)<E$ for $a(E)<q<b(E)$, and

$$U'\bigl(a(E)\bigr)<0<U'\bigl(b(E)\bigr)\qquad(E_0<E<E_1)$$

(the energy $E$ has exactly the two simple turning points $a(E)$, $b(E)$ in
$J_0$). Then:

1. $a$ and $b$ are of class $C^1$ on $(E_0,E_1)$;
2. the action variable $J_{\mathrm{a}}$ of
   [[def-cm-one-dimensional-action-variable]] is of class $C^1$ on
   $(E_0,E_1)$, and for every $E\in(E_0,E_1)$
   $$J_{\mathrm{a}}'(E)=\frac{1}{2\pi}T(E),\qquad T(E):=\sqrt{2m}\int_{a(E)}^{b(E)}\frac{\mathrm dq}{\sqrt{E-U(q)}}\in(0,\infty),$$
   where the integral is the improper integral over the open interval
   $(a(E),b(E))$, convergent at both endpoints.

references.title: David Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge), §4.5.3, printed pp. 108-111, Eqs. (4.136)-(4.142): $I=\frac1{2\pi}\oint p\,\mathrm dq$, the varying-endpoint cancellation and the identity $\mathrm dE/\mathrm dI=\omega=2\pi/T$
Konstantin Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Classical Mechanics, Ch. 10: the action variable and its energy derivative for a periodic one-dimensional motion

items.title: Scattering data: the incident flux measure, the solid-angle element, deflection branches and the cross-section density
items.design_state: completed-local-argument (E10 split into items; recorded in the batch notes)
items.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Borel/Lebesgue measure foundation below.

**Data.** Let $\mu>0$, let $U:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), let $R>0$ satisfy $U(r)=0$
for every $r\ge R$ (a **finite-range potential**), and let $E>0$ and $J>0$ be
reals. Write

$$V(r):=U(r)+\frac{J^2}{2\mu r^2}\qquad(r>0).$$

**Incident flux measure.** Let $\nu$ be the Borel measure on the open rectangle
$(0,\infty)\times(0,2\pi)$ given by the density $b$ against Lebesgue measure
$\lambda_2$,

$$\nu(A):=\int_A b\,d\lambda_2(b,\varphi)\qquad(A\subseteq(0,\infty)\times(0,2\pi)\ \text{Borel}),$$

the integral being that of [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]; the
nonnegative Borel function $(b,\varphi)\mapsto b$ defines a measure by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]
([[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]]). In the model this
measure records a uniform incident beam: an annulus of impact parameters
$[b_1,b_2)$ contributes $\pi(b_2^2-b_1^2)$ over the full azimuth range, or
$\tfrac12(b_2^2-b_1^2)$ per unit azimuth.

**Solid-angle element.** Let $\Omega$ be the Borel measure on
$(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)$ with density $\sin$ against $\lambda_2$,

$$\Omega(B):=\int_B\sin\theta\,d\lambda_2(\theta,\varphi)\qquad(B\subseteq(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)\ \text{Borel}),$$

where $\sin$ is the function of [[def-sine-and-cosine-by-power-series]]. This
is the standard solid-angle element written $\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\varphi$
(the surface measure of the unit sphere in spherical coordinates, restricted
to the open chart).

**Deflection branch.** A **deflection branch** is an interval
$(a_1,a_2)\subseteq(0,\infty)$ with at least two points together with a
function $\theta:(a_1,a_2)\to(0,\pi)$ that is of class $C^1$ and satisfies
$\theta'(b)\ne0$ for every $b\in(a_1,a_2)$. Such a $\theta$ is strictly
monotone (the continuous nonvanishing derivative has constant sign, and [[cor-mean-value-theorem]] gives strict monotonicity) and its image is an interval with endpoints $\theta_1<\theta_2$
([[def-interval]]); its inverse $b:(\theta_1,\theta_2)\to(a_1,a_2)$ is
differentiable with $b'(\theta)=1/\theta'(b(\theta))$, by the
derivative-of-an-inverse theorem [[thm-derivative-of-an-inverse]] applied to
the continuous injective $\theta$ (every point of $(a_1,a_2)$ is a limit point
of it, [[def-limit-point-r]], [[def-derivative]]).

**Cross-section density.** The **cross-section density of the branch** is the
function

$$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}(\theta):=\frac{b(\theta)}{\sin\theta\,\bigl|\theta'\bigl(b(\theta)\bigr)\bigr|} \qquad(\theta_1<\theta<\theta_2).$$

**Mathematical status.** The measures, branches and density are abstract data
independent of the finite-range trajectory data $(\mu,U,R,E,J)$. A branch is not asserted to arise from any
trajectory; the scattering theorems of this page identify the deflection
angle computed from the central-force equation with the values of such a
function under their hypotheses, and they compute the pushforward of $\nu$ under the induced map. No counting of
detected particles, and no empirical claim, is part of this definition.

references.title: Richard Fitzpatrick, Newtonian Dynamics (University of Texas at Austin), §6.4 Scattering in the Center of Mass Frame, Eqs. (340)-(367): impact parameter, turning-point quadrature, the annular incident area and outgoing solid angle
Konstantin Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Classical Mechanics, §3.5, Eqs. (3.66)-(3.72): impact parameter, scattering angle, uniform-beam counting and the geometric cross-section relation

items.title: Finite-range scattering: the simple outer turning point, the two global branches and the free tails
items.design_state: completed-local-argument (E10 split into items; recorded in the batch notes)
items.statement:
Let $\mu>0$, let $U:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$, let $R>0$ satisfy
$U(r)=0$ for every $r\ge R$, let $E>0$ and $J>0$, and put
$V(r):=U(r)+J^2/(2\mu r^2)$ ([[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]]). Suppose $r_*>0$
satisfies

$$V(r_*)=E,\qquad V'(r_*)<0,\qquad V(r)<E\quad(r>r_*).$$

Let $r:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a central-force trajectory for $(\mu,U)$ with
constant nonzero angular momentum $j=Je_3$, $J>0$, energy $E$, and
$|r(t)|\ge r_*$ for all $t\in I$, whose radial part attains the value $r_*$ at
some $t_*\in I$ ([[thm-cm-central-force-polar-reduction]]). Then:

1. $(\rho')^2=\dfrac{2}{\mu}\bigl(E-V(\rho)\bigr)$ on $I$, where $\rho=|r|$;
   $\rho'(t_*)=0$ and $\rho''(t_*)=-V'(r_*)/\mu>0$, so $t_*$ is a strict
   minimum of $\rho$;
2. $r$ extends uniquely to a central-force trajectory on all of $\mathbb R$;
   along the extension $\rho\ge r_*$, $\rho(t)>\rho(t_*)=r_*$ for $t\ne t_*$,
   and $\rho$ is strictly decreasing on $(-\infty,t_*]$ and strictly
   increasing on $[t_*,\infty)$;
3. the time quadrature
   $$\tau(r):=\int_{r_*}^{r}\frac{\mathrm ds}{\sqrt{(2/\mu)(E-V(s))}} \qquad(r\ge r_*)$$
   is finite for every $r$ and satisfies
   $\rho(t_*+\tau(r))=r$ for all $r\ge r_*$;
4. for every time $t_1\ge t_*$ with $\rho(t_1)>R$ the motion is exactly free
   from $t_1$ on: $r(t)=r(t_1)+(t-t_1)r'(t_1)$ for all $t\ge t_1$, and $\rho$
   is strictly increasing there; symmetrically, for $t_2\le t_*$ with
   $\rho(t_2)>R$, $r(t)=r(t_2)+(t-t_2)r'(t_2)$ for all $t\le t_2$.

references.title: Richard Fitzpatrick, Newtonian Dynamics (University of Texas at Austin), §6.4, Eqs. (340)-(346): the energy equation, the turning point and the two asymptotic branches of a scattering orbit

Konstantin Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Classical Mechanics, §3.5, Eqs. (3.66)-(3.68): the nearest-approach point, the equality of the two branch angle changes and the scattering-angle quadrature

items.title: Existence of the asymptotic velocities and the impact-parameter identity $J=\mu b|v_-|$
items.design_state: completed-local-argument (E10 split into items; recorded in the batch notes)
items.statement:
Let the hypotheses of
[[thm-cm-scattering-turning-point-and-global-branches]] hold, with finite-range
potential $U$, energy $E>0$, angular momentum $j=Je_3$, $J>0$, outer turning
point $r_*$, and let $r:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be the extension of the
trajectory. Then:

1. the limits $v_\pm:=\lim_{t\to\pm\infty}r'(t)$ exist and satisfy
   $|v_+|=|v_-|=\sqrt{2E/\mu}$;
2. for every $t_2\le t_*$ with $\rho(t_2)>R$, the incoming free tail is the half-line $\{r(t_2)+s\,v_-:s\le0\}$, whose affine extension is the
   straight line $\{r(t_2)+s\,v_-:s\in\mathbb R\}$; its perpendicular distance
   from the origin is
   $$b:=\frac{|r(t_2)\times v_-|}{|v_-|}=\frac{J}{\mu|v_-|}, \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad J=\mu b|v_-| .$$

references.title: Richard Fitzpatrick, Newtonian Dynamics (University of Texas at Austin), §6.4, Eqs. (340)-(346): the asymptotic velocity, the impact parameter and the relation $L=mvb$
Konstantin Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Classical Mechanics, §3.5, Eq. (3.66): $L_z=b(2mE)^{1/2}$ for a scattering orbit

items.title: The scattering angle advance $\Delta$ and the deflection relation: the total polar advance is $2\Delta$ and the velocity directions make the cosine $\cos(\pi-2\Delta)$
items.design_state: completed-local-argument (E10 split into items; recorded in the batch notes)
items.statement:
Let the hypotheses of
[[thm-cm-scattering-turning-point-and-global-branches]] hold, let
$r:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be the extension of the trajectory, and let
$(\rho,\theta)$ be polar data with $r=\rho\,n(\theta)$,
$n(\varphi)=\cos\varphi\,e_1+\sin\varphi\,e_2$
([[thm-cm-central-force-polar-reduction]]). Write
$t_*$ for the apsis time, and for $\alpha\in\mathbb R$ let $R_\alpha$ be the
rotation of the plane $\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2)$,
$R_\alpha(x):=\cos\alpha\,x+\sin\alpha\,(e_3\times x)$. Then:

1. the half-angle
   $$\Delta:=\int_{r_*}^{\infty}\frac{J\,\mathrm dr}{r^2\sqrt{2\mu\,(E-V(r))}}$$
   is finite and positive, and
   $$\theta(\infty)-\theta(t_*)=\Delta=\theta(t_*)-\theta(-\infty),\qquad \theta(\infty)-\theta(-\infty)=2\Delta;$$
2. $\displaystyle\lim_{t\to\pm\infty}n(\theta(t))$ exist and equal
   $v_+/|v_+|$ (as $t\to+\infty$) and $-v_-/|v_-|$ (as $t\to-\infty$);
3. consequently
   $$\frac{v_+}{|v_+|}=-R_{2\Delta}\Bigl(\frac{v_-}{|v_-|}\Bigr), \qquad \frac{\langle v_-,v_+\rangle}{|v_-|\,|v_+|}=-\cos 2\Delta=\cos(\pi-2\Delta);$$
   in particular, if $0<\Delta<\pi/2$ then $\pi-2\Delta\in(0,\pi)$ is the
   (undirected) angle between the asymptotic velocity directions, and the
   signed velocity rotation is $-( \pi-2\Delta)$ in the orientation defined by
   $e_3$.

references.title: Richard Fitzpatrick, Newtonian Dynamics (University of Texas at Austin), §6.4, Eqs. (346)-(351): the scattering-angle quadrature and the relation between the half-angle and the deflection
Konstantin Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Classical Mechanics, §3.5, Eqs. (3.66)-(3.68): $\theta=\pi-2\varphi_0$ with the nearest-approach angle $\varphi_0$

items.title: One-dimensional substitution on a deflection branch: the outgoing angular measure has density $b|\mathrm db/\mathrm d\theta|$, hence cross-section density $b|\mathrm db/\mathrm d\theta|/\sin\theta$
items.design_state: completed-local-argument (E10 split into items; recorded in the batch notes)
items.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$\theta:(a_1,a_2)\to(\theta_1,\theta_2)\subseteq(0,\pi)$ be a deflection
branch of [[def-cm-scattering-data]], with inverse $b(\theta)$, and set
$D=(a_1,a_2)\times(0,2\pi)$, $H=(\theta_1,\theta_2)\times(0,2\pi)$ and
$T(b,\varphi)=(\theta(b),\varphi)$. Restrict the incident measure $\nu$ to
$D$. Its pushforward, defined by $T_*\nu(B)=\nu(T^{-1}(B))$ for Borel
$B\subseteq H$, satisfies
$$T_*\nu(B)=\int_B b(\theta)|b'(\theta)|\,d\lambda_2(\theta,\varphi).$$
For every nonnegative Borel $g:H\to[0,+\infty]$, and for every real Borel
$g$ with either side's integral of $|g|$ finite, consequently
$$\int_D g(\theta(b),\varphi)b\,d\lambda_2(b,\varphi)=\int_H g(\theta,\varphi)b(\theta)|b'(\theta)|\,d\lambda_2(\theta,\varphi).$$
The nonnegative equality allows $+\infty$; in the real case both sides are
finite and absolute integrability on one side is equivalent to that on the
other. In particular it applies to continuous periodic test functions that
are nonnegative or absolutely integrable, and to compactly supported
continuous test functions. No equality of undefined signed improper
integrals is asserted. Nonnegative double-integral notation denotes the
corresponding Lebesgue integrals, with iterated integrals justified by Tonelli.

Thus the outgoing angular measure has density $b(\theta)|b'(\theta)|$
against $d\theta\,d\varphi$ and density
$$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}(\theta)=\frac{b(\theta)|b'(\theta)|}{\sin\theta}=\frac{b(\theta)}{\sin\theta\,|\theta'(b(\theta))|}$$
against the solid-angle measure. For finitely many branches on disjoint
incident intervals the measures add, including on overlapping image
intervals; in particular contributions with pairwise disjoint images add.

references.title: Richard Fitzpatrick, Newtonian Dynamics (University of Texas at Austin), §6.4, Eqs. (347)-(351): the annular incident area $2\pi b\,\mathrm db$ and the outgoing solid angle, giving $\mathrm d\sigma/\mathrm d\Omega=(b/\sin\theta)|\mathrm db/\mathrm d\theta|$

Konstantin Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Classical Mechanics, §3.5, Eqs. (3.70)-(3.72): the differential cross-section and the geometric relation $\mathrm d\sigma/\mathrm d\Omega=b|\mathrm db/\mathrm d\theta|/\sin\theta$

items.title: Repulsive Coulomb scattering: the unique outer turning point, global non-colliding motion, the asymptotic impact distance and $\Delta=\pi/2-\arctan(\kappa/(2Eb))$
items.design_state: completed-local-argument (E10 split into items; recorded in the batch notes)
items.statement:
Let $\mu>0$, let $\kappa>0$ and $U(r)=\kappa/r$ on $(0,\infty)$ (the repulsive
Coulomb potential, of class $C^2$), let $E>0$ and $J>0$, and put
$$V(r):=\frac{\kappa}{r}+\frac{J^2}{2\mu r^2},\qquad b:=\frac{J}{\sqrt{2\mu E}}>0,\qquad \alpha:=\frac{\kappa}{Eb}>0.$$
Then:

1. $V$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,\infty)$, with $V(r)\to\infty$ as $r\downarrow0$
   and $V(r)\to0$ as $r\to\infty$; hence there is exactly one $r_*>0$ with
   $V(r_*)=E$, it is simple ($V'(r_*)<0$), and $V(r)<E$ for all $r>r_*$.
2. Let $r:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a central-force trajectory for $(\mu,U)$ with
   constant angular momentum $j=Je_3$, $J>0$, energy $E$, with $|r(t)|\ge r_*$
   for all $t\in I$ and with $|r(t_*)|=r_*$ for some $t_*\in I$. Then $r$
   extends uniquely to all of $\mathbb R$; along the extension $\rho=|r|\ge r_*>0$
   (no collision), $\rho$ is strictly decreasing on $(-\infty,t_*]$ and
   strictly increasing on $[t_*,\infty)$, and the asymptotic velocities
   $v_\pm=\lim_{t\to\pm\infty}r'(t)$ exist with $|v_+|=|v_-|=\sqrt{2E/\mu}$.
   Moreover the asymptotic perpendicular distance of each branch to its
   limiting direction exists and equals
   $$b=\frac{J}{\sqrt{2\mu E}}=\frac{J}{\mu|v_\pm|}, \qquad\text{so that}\qquad J=\mu b|v_\pm| .$$
The distance in clause 2 means the limit of $|r(t)\times v_\pm|/|v_\pm|$ as $t\to\pm\infty$, the distance to the line through the origin in the limiting velocity direction; it does not assert a free tail or a finite longitudinal intercept.

3. For the polar angle, with $u_*:=1/r_*$,
   $$\Delta:=\int_{r_*}^{\infty}\frac{J\,\mathrm dr}{r^2\sqrt{2\mu\,(E-V(r))}} =\int_0^{u_*}\frac{b\,\mathrm du}{\sqrt{1-\dfrac{\kappa}{E}u-b^2u^2}} =\frac{\pi}{2}-\arctan\frac{\kappa}{2Eb}.$$

4. Write $n_\pm=\lim_{t\to\pm\infty}r(t)/|r(t)|$. Then
   $n_+=v_+/|v_+|$, $n_-=-v_-/|v_-|$, and in an oriented polar plane
   the outgoing velocity direction is the incoming direction rotated by
   $2\Delta-\pi\in(-\pi,0)$. In particular
   $$\frac{\langle v_-,v_+\rangle}{|v_-||v_+|}=\cos(\pi-2\Delta),\qquad \theta_{\mathrm s}=\pi-2\Delta=2\arctan\frac{\kappa}{2Eb}.$$
   For fixed $\mu,\kappa,E$ this gives an actual family for every $b>0$,
   with angular momentum $J(b)=\sqrt{2\mu E}\,b$: choose its unique turning
   radius and initial data $r(0)=r_*e_1$, $r'(0)=J(b)e_2/(\mu r_*)$.
   Local existence and the extension in clause 2 give a member of the family
   for every $b$, unique up to apsis time and oriented plane placement.

references.title: Richard Fitzpatrick, Newtonian Dynamics (University of Texas at Austin), §6.4, Eqs. (358)-(366): the inverse-square scattering integral, the Rutherford angle relation and the asymptotic distance
Konstantin Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Classical Mechanics, §3.5, Eqs. (3.68)-(3.69): the scattering integral for the Coulomb potential, $\tan(\theta/2)=\alpha/(2Eb)$

items.title: The Rutherford deflection map, its inverse, the cross-section density $(\kappa/4E)^2\csc^4(\theta/2)$ and the divergence of the total cross-section
items.design_state: completed-local-argument (E10 split into items; recorded in the batch notes)
items.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the cross-section measures. Fix $\mu>0$, $\kappa>0$ and $E>0$. For every $b>0$ put $J(b)=\sqrt{2\mu E}\,b$ and use the Coulomb trajectory family of [[thm-cm-coulomb-scattering]] clause 4. Its impact distance is $b$ and its
**deflection map**
$$\theta_{\rm def}:(0,\infty)\to(0,\pi),\qquad \theta_{\rm def}(b):=2\arctan\frac{\kappa}{2Eb}.$$
Then:

1. $\theta_{\rm def}$ is $C^1$ and strictly decreasing, with
   $\theta_{\rm def}(b)\to\pi$ as $b\downarrow0$ and
   $\theta_{\rm def}(b)\to0$ as $b\to\infty$; it is a $C^1$ bijection
   $(0,\infty)\to(0,\pi)$ with inverse
   $$b(\theta)=\frac{\kappa}{2E}\cot\frac{\theta}{2}\qquad(0<\theta<\pi).$$
2. For every interval $(\theta_1,\theta_2)\subseteq(0,\pi)$ the pair
   $(\theta,b)$ is a deflection branch with cross-section density
   $$\frac{\mathrm d\sigma}{\mathrm d\Omega}(\theta) =b(\theta)\Bigl|\frac{\mathrm db}{\mathrm d\theta}(\theta)\Bigr|\frac{1}{\sin\theta} =\Bigl(\frac{\kappa}{4E}\Bigr)^2\csc^4\frac{\theta}{2},$$
   finite and positive on $(\theta_1,\theta_2)$; and the pushforward of the
   incident flux measure under the branch is described by
   [[thm-cm-differential-cross-section-density]].
3. For every $\theta_0\in(0,\pi)$ the truncated total cross-section
   $$\int_0^{\theta_0}\!\!\int_0^{2\pi}\Bigl(\frac{\kappa}{4E}\Bigr)^2 \csc^4\frac{\theta}{2}\,\sin\theta\,\mathrm d\varphi\,\mathrm d\theta=+\infty,$$
   while for $0<\theta_1<\theta_2<\pi$ the integral over
   $(\theta_1,\theta_2)\times(0,2\pi)$ is finite; in this sense the total
   cross-section of the ideal Coulomb model diverges at forward angles and
   every compact angular acceptance away from $0$ has finite cross-section.

references.title: Richard Fitzpatrick, Newtonian Dynamics (University of Texas at Austin), §6.4, Eqs. (358)-(367): the Rutherford cross-section and the small-angle divergence of the total cross-section
Konstantin Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Classical Mechanics, §3.5, Eq. (3.69) and following: $\tan(\theta/2)=\alpha/(2Eb)$ and the Rutherford scattering formula

items.title: The harmonic oscillator action variable $J_{\mathrm a}(E)=E/\omega$ and $J_{\mathrm a}'(E)=T/(2\pi)$
items.design_state: completed-local-argument (E6 split into items; recorded in the batch notes)
items.statement:
Let $m>0$, $k>0$, $U(q)=\frac12kq^2$ on $J_0=\mathbb R$, and for $E>0$ set
$$a(E):=-\sqrt{\frac{2E}{k}},\qquad b(E):=\sqrt{\frac{2E}{k}},\qquad \omega:=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}},\qquad T:=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}.$$
Then the datum $(J_0,U,m,a,b)$ satisfies the hypotheses of
[[thm-cm-action-variable-derivative]] on the energy interval $(0,\infty)$, the
action variable of [[def-cm-one-dimensional-action-variable]] is
$$J_{\mathrm a}(E)=\frac{E}{\omega}\qquad(E>0),$$
and
$$J_{\mathrm a}'(E)=\frac{1}{\omega}=\frac{T}{2\pi}\qquad(E>0),$$
in agreement with the general theorem, whose period quadrature is
$T(E)=\sqrt{2m}\int_{a(E)}^{b(E)}\mathrm dq/\sqrt{E-U(q)}=2\pi/\omega$.

references.title: David Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge), §4.5.1 and §4.5.3, printed pp. 105-111: the harmonic oscillator action variable and the period relation $\mathrm dE/\mathrm dI=\omega$

items.title: An exact Kepler ellipse check: $e=1/2$, $J=1$, $\mu=\kappa=1$ give $a=4/3$, $b=2\sqrt3/3$, $E=-3/8$ and $T^2=256\pi^2/27$
items.design_state: completed-local-argument (E6 split into items; recorded in the batch notes)
items.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), as required by the conic, ellipse and period suppliers.

Take the attractive Kepler data $\mu=\kappa=1$ and angular momentum magnitude
$J=1$, and consider the negative-energy orbit with eccentricity $e=\frac12$.
Then the conic data of [[thm-cm-kepler-conic-and-eccentricity]] and
[[thm-cm-kepler-ellipse-geometry]] are
$$p=\frac{J^2}{\mu\kappa}=1,\qquad a=\frac{p}{1-e^2}=\frac43,\qquad b=a\sqrt{1-e^2}=\frac{2\sqrt3}{3},$$
the energy is $E=\dfrac{\mu\kappa^2}{2J^2}(e^2-1)=-\dfrac38$, and the period of
[[thm-cm-kepler-orbit-period]] satisfies
$$T=\frac{2\pi\mu ab}{J}=\frac{16\pi\sqrt3}{9},\qquad T^2=\frac{256\pi^2}{27}=\frac{4\pi^2\mu a^3}{\kappa}.$$
All numbers are exact; the example checks algebraic consistency of the three
theorems and the sign criterion $E<0\iff e<1$, and makes no empirical claim.

references.title: Konstantin Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Classical Mechanics, §3.4, Eqs. (3.59)-(3.65): the eccentricity, semimajor axis and period relations checked numerically here with exact rational data

items.title: An exact Rutherford check: $\kappa=E=1$, $b=1$ give $\theta=2\arctan\frac12$ and $\mathrm d\sigma/\mathrm d\Omega=25/16$
items.design_state: completed-local-argument (E10 split into items; recorded in the batch notes)
items.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the cited scattering measures and vocabulary.

Take the repulsive Coulomb data $\kappa=1$ and $E=1$ (with any $\mu>0$ and
$J=\sqrt{2\mu}$, so that the asymptotic impact distance of
[[thm-cm-coulomb-scattering]] is $b=1$). Then the deflection map of
[[thm-cm-rutherford-cross-section]] has the exact values
$$\theta_{\rm def}(1)=2\arctan\frac12\in(0,\pi), \qquad \frac{\pi}{2}-\Delta=\arctan\frac12,\qquad \Delta=\frac{\pi}{2}-\arctan\frac12,$$
the inverse branch satisfies $b(\theta_{\rm def}(1))=1$, and
$$\frac{\mathrm d\sigma}{\mathrm d\Omega}\Bigl(\theta_{\rm def}(1)\Bigr) =\Bigl(\frac{\kappa}{4E}\Bigr)^2\csc^4\Bigl(\frac{\theta_{\rm def}(1)}{2}\Bigr) =\frac{25}{16},$$
because $\theta_{\rm def}(1)/2=\arctan\frac12$ and $\csc^2(\arctan\frac12)=1+\cot^2(\arctan\frac12)=1+4=5$.

references.title: Richard Fitzpatrick, Newtonian Dynamics (University of Texas at Austin), §6.4, Eqs. (358)-(365): the Rutherford angle and density, checked here at exact rational data

items.title: A zero-angular-momentum Kepler trajectory reaches the force centre in finite time, refuting unconditional global existence
items.design_state: completed-local-argument (E10 split into items; recorded in the batch notes)
items.statement:
**False statement.** *Every solution of the attractive inverse-square equation
$\mu\,r''=-\kappa\,r/|r|^3$ ($\mu,\kappa>0$) on its maximal interval of
definition is defined for all real times and satisfies $|r(t)|\ge c$ for some
$c>0$.*

The witness has zero angular momentum and reaches the excluded force centre;
non-radial orbit results therefore cannot be applied to it. It also shows why
the finite-range scattering theorem
[[thm-cm-scattering-turning-point-and-global-branches]] assumes a simple
turning point rather than mere boundedness from below.

references.title: David Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge), §2.5.4, printed pp. 32-33: the angular-momentum barrier and the separation of the radial and angular problems
